questions.knowledge_point: Partial Derivatives as Limits of Difference Quotients
questions.worked_solution:
The derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by the limit 

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{f(x,y+h)-f(x,y)}{h}).
$$

Since $f(x)={x}^{y},$  we have that 

$$
f(x,y+h)={x}^{y+h}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{{x}^{y+h}-{x}^{y}}{h}).
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The notation ${f}_{x}$ denotes the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x.$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{y}^{4}}+6xy) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{y}^{4}})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{4}}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})+6y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{4}}\cdot 3{x}^{2}+6y\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{y}^{4}}+6y\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Partial Derivative at a Point
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-xy) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-y\cdot (1) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,\pi ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡0-\pi  \\  & =(-1)\cdot 1-\pi  \\  & =-\pi -1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=2x\sqrt{y}-4y\sqrt{x},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\sqrt{y}-4y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\sqrt{y})-\frac{∂}{∂x}(4y\sqrt{x}) \\  & =2\sqrt{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-4y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =2\sqrt{y}\cdot (1)-4y\cdot (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{y}-\frac{2y}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,4)} & =2\sqrt{4}-\frac{2\cdot 4}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =4-8 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(\pi ,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡y-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)-x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{y})-x\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{y}-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi ,\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(\pi ,\pi /2)} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }{(\frac{\pi }{2})}-\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\pi }-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}\sqrt{x}+\frac{x}{y},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(4,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}\sqrt{x}+\frac{x}{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}\sqrt{x}+x{y}^{-1}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}\sqrt{x})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{-1}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})+x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{-1}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (2y)+x\cdot (-{y}^{-2}) \\  & =2y\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(4,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(4,2)} & =2\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{4}-4\cdot {2}^{-2} \\  & =8-1 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Partial Derivatives as Limits of Difference Quotients
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $f(x,y) = y^2\ln{x},$ express $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ as the limit of a difference quotient.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by the limit 

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)}{h}\right).
$$

Since $f(x) = y^2 \ln{x},$  we have that 

$$
f(x+h,y) = y^2\ln(x+h).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0}\left( \dfrac{y^2\ln(x+h) -y^2\ln{x} }{h}\right).
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ given that $f(x,y) = 3x\ln y + 2ye^x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y{e}^{x}) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+2{e}^{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y) \\  & =3x\cdot \frac{1}{y}+2{e}^{x}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3x}{y}+2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y) = x^2y^2+\sin{x}\cos{y},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(\pi,2\pi).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot (2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2x{y}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi,2\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,2\pi )} & =2\cdot \pi \cdot (2\pi )^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2\pi \cdot 4{\pi }^{2}+(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =8{\pi }^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$
